story.headline: Asian markets turned cautious ahead of expected new US tariffs, so the dollar edged up and the Australian dollar gave back its jump on hot inflation. US core inflation comes out at 7:30 AM CT.

reads.policy: A December Fed hike is fully priced, so the dollar now needs bets on further hikes to rise much more. Hot Australian inflation ended talk of a cut there, and Canada and the UK still lean toward December hikes. In Japan, mixed inflation signals keep a December hike likely but not certain.
reads.growth: Germany's economy grew a touch less than first reported in the third quarter, a reminder that its recovery is slow. US growth and spending figures on Wednesday will show whether the US economy is still outrunning the rest, which has kept the dollar strong.
reads.inflation: Inflation is running hot in Australia and still above target in Japan, which keeps those central banks from easing. US core inflation for October, out Wednesday morning, is the week's biggest test for the dollar.
reads.risk: Asian markets turned cautious ahead of expected new US tariffs on 16 trading partners. Money went into the dollar this time, while riskier currencies like the Aussie and kiwi fell. Gold slid too, a sign that higher US rates still outweigh fear.
reads.tot: Oil slipped back under $90 as rising supply outweighed worries about Gulf attacks, a small drag on the Canadian dollar. Gold's slide takes away some support from Australia's export earnings.
reads.positioning: The latest weekly figures show hedge funds have turned slightly against the dollar, while still betting against the euro, the kiwi, the franc and, most strongly, the Canadian dollar. They still bet on the pound and the Aussie, where big long-term investors take the opposite side. Where the two groups disagree, a surprise could set off a fast unwind.
reads.fiscal: The US is expected to unveil new tariffs on 16 trading partners, including China, the European Union and Japan, which could weigh on their economies and on US growth. Record US government borrowing keeps long-term US borrowing costs high. France's debts remain a weight on the euro, with S&P due to review its credit rating on Friday.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike, and most officials now expect more hikes. Traders fully expect a quarter-point hike in December, with another one in January more likely than not.
fed.priced: December: quarter-point hike fully expected. January: another hike more likely than not.
fed.why: US inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal, and consumer confidence jumped in November to its highest since January 2025. That gives the Fed little reason to hold back.
fed.watch: Core inflation for October, the second estimate of third-quarter growth and the Beige Book on Wednesday, November 25. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October. Governor Tiff Macklem said on Tuesday, November 24 the bank would hike again if inflation stays too high for too long, and a December hike now looks likely.
boc.why: Macklem expects inflation to end the year a little lower as oil eased, but warned the oil shock will keep prices sticky. He said the bank may need to act sooner or harder.
boc.watch: Canada's third-quarter growth on Monday, November 30, the jobs report on Friday, December 4, and oil prices. The decision is December 9.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a narrow vote. Rising unemployment has made a December hike less certain, but a jump in shop sales in the third quarter strengthens the case for one.
rbnz.priced: December: hike possible but not fully expected.
rbnz.why: Inflation pressures and stronger spending argue for a hike, while unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for waiting. Governor Anna Breman gave no clear signal on December in her latest speech.
rbnz.watch: The official election result on Friday, November 27 and the next dairy price auction. The decision is December 9.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held at 2.50% in October and a December hike is widely expected. Euro-area inflation is about double its goal, but the euro sits near its weakest in about 19 months as US rates rise faster.
ecb.priced: December: hike widely expected, possibly the last for a while.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal and core prices are firming. Slow German growth, weak factories and France's debts limit how far it can go.
ecb.watch: The accounts of the October meeting on Thursday, November 26 at 6:30 AM CT, and S&P's review of France's credit rating on Friday, November 27. The decision is December 17.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan holds at 1.25%, far below other major banks, and is expected to hike in December. Inflation is above its 2% goal, but the dollar still trades near 159 yen because US rates keep rising faster.
boj.why: Inflation has stayed above 2%, and prices firms charge each other for services are rising fast. But the bank's own core inflation measure cooled in October, one reason some, such as JPMorgan, see December as closer to a coin flip.
boj.watch: Tokyo's November inflation on Thursday, November 26 at 5:30 PM CT, and any sign Japan steps in near 160 yen. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest among the major banks. Inflation jumped to 4.9% in October, which ended bets on a cut soon, though job losses argue against another hike.
rba.priced: December: hold expected. Cuts in 2027 now look less likely.
rba.why: Inflation is well above the bank's 2–3% target and rising, but job losses and shrinking business activity argue for patience. That leaves the bank holding, with the risk now leaning toward another hike rather than a cut.
rba.watch: Australian business investment on Wednesday, November 25 at 6:30 PM CT and any comments from bank officials. The decision is December 8.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5. Policymaker Megan Greene said on Tuesday, November 24 that the fall in inflation has stalled and another hike is warranted, a day after chief economist Huw Pill said the bank must act now.
boe.why: High fuel costs from the Middle East conflict keep UK inflation near twice the bank's goal, and pay growth is stuck above a comfortable pace. Greene said the bank is a little behind.
boe.watch: Officials answer lawmakers' questions on Wednesday, November 25 at 2:15 PM CT, then the Financial Stability Report on Thursday, November 26 at 4:30 AM CT. The decision is December 17.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and can sell francs if they get too strong. Low Swiss inflation means no hike is in sight.
snb.why: Swiss inflation is low, so the bank has no reason to raise rates and some room to cut if the franc climbs.
snb.watch: Any flare-up in stock markets or the Gulf that sends money into the franc. The decision is December 10.

GBP.summary: The pound sits at the top of the board because UK interest rates are among the highest of the eight, and the Bank of England sounds ready to hike again in December. It still trades near a one-year low against the dollar.

AUD.summary: The Aussie sits second on the board, thanks to the highest interest rates among the major central banks. Inflation jumped in October, which makes rate cuts less likely, but job losses and nervous markets keep it near its lowest in a year.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits third on the board. Firm dairy prices and strong shop sales help, but doubts over a December rate hike and a firm US dollar keep it near a 17-year low.

USD.summary: The dollar sits fourth, in the middle of the board. High US interest rates support it, while large budget deficits weigh. It trades a little below its 20-month high, with a December Fed hike fully expected.

EUR.summary: The euro sits fifth, just below the middle of the board. Germany's economy is recovering only slowly, and France's debts hold the euro back. It trades near $1.095, not far above its weakest in about 19 months.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits sixth, in the lower half of the board. Cheaper oil than a month ago hurts Canada's exports and recent data has mostly missed forecasts, though a likely December Bank of Canada hike now gives it some support.

JPY.summary: The yen sits second from the bottom because Japanese interest rates are far below the others. A likely December Bank of Japan hike offers some hope, but the dollar trades near 159 yen.

CHF.summary: The franc sits at the bottom of the board. Swiss interest rates are the lowest of the eight and inflation is too low to need higher rates. It gains mainly when fear in markets sends safe-haven money its way.
